newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan minister raps Transport Ministry on car parts.
newsitem.headline: Japan minister raps Transport Ministry on car parts.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's criticism of Japanese efforts to deregulate its car parts industry sparked a finger-pointing exercise between Japan's Trade and Transport ministries on Monday.
Trade Minister Shinji Sato, stung by Albright's comments to him on the issue during talks in Tokyo on Sunday, turned the heat on the country's Transport Ministry.
"I think the Transport Ministry could deregulate a little more," Sato told a news conference in reply to a question on the Transport Ministry's rules on brakes.
Albright told Sato that failure to fully implement a 1995 bilateral auto accord could lead to trade friction.
Sato pledged to Albright that Japan will live up to the agreement which calls for greater deregulation of Japan's lucrative auto parts markets.
The Transport Ministry refused to get dragged into a debate, commenting only that "the (trade) minister was probably speaking in general terms and not specifically about any particular regulation".
Washington has said it is disappointed with the decision by Japan's Transport Ministry earlier this month denying relaxation of rules on brake part repairs for safety reasons.

"The decision of the Japanese government is a move in exactly the wrong direction and only makes deregulation of Japan's (service) garage system even more important," U.S. Trade Representative Designate Charlene Barshefsky said in a statement at the time.
The U.S. car parts industry requested that brakes be removed from the ministry's list of parts that require servicing by a government-approved garage.
But the ministry refused, saying that "it would make it possible for repairs to be carried out by people other than mechanics".
Under the 1995 agreement, the U.S. car parts industry may lodge a protest with Japan's Transport Ministry against the decision.

U.S. officials have also said they are disappointed with the "resistance" encountered by the U.S. Big Three car makers in opening dealerships. Only 124 dealerships have been opened compared with their original goal of 200 one year after the accord, they said. Washington says that while there has been progress in its long tussle with Tokyo over improving access to Japan's car market, foreign import penetration of the vehicle market stands at only six percent and at only three percent for auto parts.
